intro: Copland’s Orchestral Variations is his orchestration of his 1930 piano work, twenty variations and a coda built on four notes, E, C, E♭ and C♯. A soft horn plays the ringing C♯ of the opening, and parts of the keyboard’s hard-edged lines become a duet for flute and oboe.

sections.label: Variation 11 · Woodwind variation at the centre

cues.title: Four-note motif and held C♯
cues.text: The whole piece is built from four notes, E, C, E♭ and C♯. In the piano original a key held down silently lets C♯ ring on after the other notes are struck. In the orchestral version a horn holds that note softly after a clang of brass and percussion.
cues.evidence: Kyle Gann’s American Symphony Orchestra note identifies the four-note idea and explains how the horn takes over the piano’s sympathetic resonance. https://americansymphony.org/concert-notes/orchestral-variantions-1957/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Theme and first variation
cues.text: Copland reverses the usual order of a variation set. The theme is stated forcefully, and the first variation is more subdued. The same four notes form a hard chord in one place and a line passed between instruments in another.
cues.evidence: Barbara Heninger’s Redwood Symphony note explains the reversal between the forceful theme and the subdued first variation; Sidney Finkelstein’s Vanguard sleeve note discusses the lyricism disclosed by the orchestration. https://redwoodsymphony.org/piece/orchestral-variations/
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Orchestration and première, Louisville, 1957
cues.text: Copland wrote the piano piece in 1930 and returned to it in 1957 for a Louisville Orchestra commission. Robert Whitney conducted the orchestral première in Louisville on 5 March 1957.
cues.evidence: The Aaron Copland Fund’s work catalogue documents the piano original, the orchestration, the commission and the première. https://www.aaroncopland.com/works/orchestral-variations/

cues.title: Variation XI, flute and oboe
cues.text: The middle of the piece is a slow, quiet passage for woodwind. In the eleventh variation flute and oboe play the four-note idea as a duet. The quicker variations begin in Variation XII.
cues.evidence: Kyle Gann identifies the flute-and-oboe duet in Variation XI and the build beginning in Variation XII; Heninger describes the slow, quiet woodwind centre. https://americansymphony.org/concert-notes/orchestral-variantions-1957/ ; https://redwoodsymphony.org/piece/orchestral-variations/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Later variations, rhythmic interplay
cues.text: In the later variations quick notes pass between the instruments. One rhythm is set against another, and the beat drops away and is caught up again. The opening four notes remain underneath the changes of pace.
cues.evidence: Heninger describes the quick figures and rhythmic changes of Variations XII–XIX. Finkelstein’s Vanguard sleeve note describes the interplay of rhythms, especially from Variation XV onwards. https://redwoodsymphony.org/piece/orchestral-variations/ ; https://archive.org/download/lp_three-jewish-poems-for-orchestra-fanfare_ernest-bloch-aaron-copland-the-hartford-sy/lp_three-jewish-poems-for-orchestra-fanfare_ernest-bloch-aaron-copland-the-hartford-sy_djvu.txt
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Percussion in the orchestral score
cues.text: The orchestral score adds bongos, conga drum and cowbell to a percussion group that also includes tubular bells, glockenspiel and xylophone.
cues.evidence: The Aaron Copland Fund’s catalogue lists the percussion instruments in the 1957 orchestral version. https://www.aaroncopland.com/works/orchestral-variations/

cues.title: Coda
cues.text: The coda expands the short exchanges into heavy chords for full orchestra. Brass and percussion return to the force of the opening. The coda follows twenty variations, all built from the same four notes.
cues.evidence: Heninger describes the last variations building towards a full-orchestra coda; the Vanguard sleeve identifies the complete sequence as twenty variations and coda. https://redwoodsymphony.org/piece/orchestral-variations/ ; https://archive.org/download/lp_three-jewish-poems-for-orchestra-fanfare_ernest-bloch-aaron-copland-the-hartford-sy/lp_three-jewish-poems-for-orchestra-fanfare_ernest-bloch-aaron-copland-the-hartford-sy_djvu.txt
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.background:
The Copland family lived above and beside their department store on Washington Avenue in Brooklyn. Aaron, born on 14 November 1900, was the youngest of Sarah and Harris Copland’s five children. His parents were Russian-born Jewish immigrants, and everyone in the family helped in the shop. His sister Laurine gave him his first piano lessons. When he wanted professional lessons, his parents let him find a teacher and agreed to pay. By 1917 he was crossing the Brooklyn Bridge to study harmony and counterpoint with Rubin Goldmark.

At Fontainebleau in 1921 a friend persuaded him to sit in on Nadia Boulanger’s harmony class. She became his composition teacher, and the year he had planned to spend abroad stretched to three. In Paris he encountered Stravinsky’s music and heard the latest concert works. Boulanger took him to meet Serge Koussevitzky, who was about to take over the Boston Symphony Orchestra. After the visit Koussevitzky commissioned a symphony with Boulanger herself as organ soloist.
